newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian activists complain of harassment.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian activists complain of harassment.

text.p: Indonesian activists accused the government on Friday of a campaign of harassment, intimidation and violence against non-governmental organisations (NGOs) since riots in Jakarta last July.

More than 20 leading activist groups met for about two hours with members of the official National Human Rights Commission to lodge a complaint over what they said was a range of harassment including unauthorised detention and torture.

"Recently, non-government groups have been interrogated as witnesses by authorities, some have been terrorised and tortured," Bambang Widjojanto, head of the Indonesian Legal Aid Institute (LBH), told the commission.

Emmy Hafild, executive director of the environment group Walhi, said her group and activist groups in general had been accused of inciting violent acts, such as the riots in Jakarta and the recent kidnapping of 13 people in Irian Jaya.
A police spokesman could not be reached for comment on the accusations.
The government has blamed the July 27 riots on the small leftist People's Democratic Party (PRD), most of whose leaders are in detention facing subversion charges that carry the death penalty.
"If we have done any wrong they should take us to court, not spread disinformation," Hafild told the commission.
The Jakarta riots followed a police raid on the opposition Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) headquarters to evict supporters of ousted party leader Megawati Sukarnoputri.
Megawati is suing the government, military, police and political rivals over the issue.

Senior military officers have publicly blamed Walhi and associated NGOs in Irian Jaya for the August 14 kidnapping of 13 forestry workers near Timika in the remote province. Three workers are believed to still be in captivity. Walhi denies the charge.
The NGO delegation presented written and oral testimony that the offices of activist groups had been raided by unidentified officials and kept under surveillance.

The Jakarta-based Women's Solidarity (SP) group involved with women migrant workers said its office had been raided early on the morning of August 31. It said three staff members were detained and files and property seized.

The commission was told that one activist, Wahju Susilo, who colleagues said was too afraid to attend the commission, was stripped to his underwear before being given electric shocks, had his head put in a bucket and was punched.

East Jakarta police chief Lieutenant-Colonel Gories Mere told the Jakarta Post daily on Tuesday when asked about the raid on the Women's Solidarity office: "We have nothing to do with the raid and have no idea about it."
Commission deputy chairman Marzuki Darusman told the NGOs to report all intimidation to the police.
Commission member Asmara Nababan said the commission hoped to complete its final report on the July riots this month.
It was the worst violence Jakarta had seen in two decades.
In an interim report on August 31, the commission said it had confirmed at least five people died in the riots, 149 were injured and 74 people were still missing.
